items.subtype_name: Is the sentence asking or telling?
items.stimulus: In 2019, paleobotanist Inès Varga examined a slab of 300-million-year-old shale taken from a coal seam in Kentucky. Preserved in the rock were the fronds of an extinct seed fern, their edges lined with tiny pale dots. Varga set out to determine whether ______ The dots, she later concluded, were the remains of glands that had once secreted a sticky fluid.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the dots were damage caused by insects?
were the dots damage caused by insects.
the dots were damage caused by insects.
were the dots damage caused by insects?
items.explanation: This sentence doesn't ask anything. It reports what Varga set out to determine, so it is a statement and ends with a period. The reported question after "whether" keeps normal order, with the subject ("the dots") before the verb ("were").

A.why: You got the word order right, but you let "whether" pull you toward a question mark. The sentence only reports Varga's question, so it is a statement and needs a period.

B.why: You ended with a period, which is right, but you inverted the subject and verb. Only a direct question puts the verb first. A question reported after "whether" keeps subject-then-verb order: "the dots were."

D.why: You made both mistakes the trap sets up. You inverted the word order and you added a question mark, as if the sentence were asking a direct question. It is a statement reporting what Varga wanted to find out.

did the workshops manage to store so many designs.
the workshops managed to store so many designs?
did the workshops manage to store so many designs?
items.explanation: The sentence tells you what Arceneaux studied. It does not ask a question itself, so it ends with a period. The reported question after "how" uses ordinary statement order, with the subject ("the workshops") followed by the verb ("managed").

C.why: The word order is correct, but the question word "how" led you to a question mark. The sentence reports what the historian wanted to learn, so it is a statement and takes a period.

items.subtype_name: Is the sentence asking or telling?
items.stimulus: Excavators at a hillside settlement in southern Portugal have uncovered more than sixty clay loom weights, each pierced by a single hole. Oddly, nearly all of them lay in just two rooms. Was weaving an ordinary household chore in the village, or had it become a specialized trade? Archaeologist Rui Mendes, who has catalogued similar finds across the Iberian Peninsula, now wants to know ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: whether the two rooms had served as shared workshops?
whether had the two rooms served as shared workshops.
whether the two rooms had served as shared workshops.
whether had the two rooms served as shared workshops?
items.explanation: The question in the passage that ends with a question mark comes in an earlier sentence. The sentence with the blank reports what Mendes wants to know, so it is a statement. The reported question keeps subject-then-verb order ('the two rooms had served') and ends with a period. That is C.

B.why: You chose the right end mark but flipped the verb in front of the subject ('had the two rooms served'). Only a direct question does that. After 'whether' in a reported question, the subject comes first: 'the two rooms had served'.

D.why: You made both mistakes the choices set up. You turned the reported question into a direct one by flipping the word order, and you ended a statement with a question mark. The earlier direct question in the passage doesn't carry over to this sentence.

items.subtype_name: Is the sentence asking or telling?
items.stimulus: When the city council of Harlow proposed cutting Delmar Avenue from four lanes to two, residents of the surrounding neighborhoods worried that diverted cars would pour onto their quiet blocks. Before scheduling a vote, the council asked its transportation consultants—a firm that had redesigned similar corridors in three other cities—to estimate ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: how much traffic the narrower avenue would send onto side streets.
how much traffic would the narrower avenue send onto side streets?
how much traffic the narrower avenue would send onto side streets?
how much traffic would the narrower avenue send onto side streets.
items.explanation: If you skip over the part between the dashes, the sentence reads 'the council asked its transportation consultants to estimate how much traffic...'. It reports a request, so it is a statement and ends with a period. The reported question keeps normal order, with the subject 'the narrower avenue' before the verb 'would send'. Only A does both.

B.why: You read 'asked' and 'how much' as signs of a direct question, so you flipped the word order and added a question mark. The sentence reports what the council asked for, so it is a statement.

C.why: You got the word order right, but the question word 'how' pulled you to a question mark. The sentence states what the consultants were asked to estimate, so it needs a period.

D.why: You were right to use a period, but you put the verb 'would' before the subject 'the narrower avenue'. That order belongs only in a direct question. In a reported one, the subject comes before 'would send'.
